Your website tells one version of you.
AI tools may look for a second opinion.

Showing up in an AI answer isn't the same as being recommended in it. A tool can cite your page as a source and still point the renter to the community down the street. What others say about you can be part of what tips that choice.

Any business can call itself the best in its market. It carries more weight when an independent source says something about you, and these tools tend to take that into account along with what's on your own site.

That's the reason local news, trade publications and professional groups matter here. That coverage usually comes from someone with no reason to flatter you.

Reporters are often short on time and sources, which is an opening. A short email can work: "We saw renter questions about parking double this quarter across our communities. I think it reflects tighter street parking downtown. Happy to talk today." (Example only.)

That's different from a press release about a new amenity, which is often harder to turn into a story. A pitch like that won't land every time, and nobody can promise you a placement.

Plenty of communities run a year end special, and plenty of renters will see it in three or four places before they call.

If the website says it ends December 31, the Google profile shows it with no date, and a listing site still has last month's version, the renter has to guess which one is true. Guessing rarely builds trust. (The tag on this graphic is an example.)

Before the last two weeks of the year, it is worth checking that the offer reads the same everywhere, with the same end date, and that anything expired is taken down the day it ends. On Google, a special fits best in an offer post with its own dates.

Many leasing offices slow down or close for a few days around the holidays.
Renter searches do not.

People home for the break often use the time to browse, compare and save a few favorites for January. Whatever the Google profile, the website and the listing sites say that week is what they remember when they come back.

Before the office closes, I would check four things: holiday hours set for each date on Google, the special worded the same everywhere with its end date, photos that look current, and a tour link that works without a callback.

The listing keeps working while the team rests. It helps if it is telling the truth.

The leasing office might be closed on Christmas Eve. The apartment search keeps going.

The days between the holidays can be a natural time to browse, with time off and conversations about the year ahead. Favorites saved that week often turn into January tours, so what a renter sees then tends to stick.

A last pass before the break helps: special hours entered for every holiday date, one version of the current special with its end date, photos that reflect the community today, and a booking link that does not depend on a callback.
